text: System analysis reasoning falls into two complementary modes. Inductive analysis reasons from the particular to the general: it postulates a specific component condition or initiating fault and traces forward to determine the effect on the whole system, answering 'what happens if this occurs?' Deductive analysis reasons from the general to the particular: it postulates a defined system state, usually a failure, and works backward to identify the combinations of more basic faults that could produce it. Fault tree analysis is a deductive technique. Inductive methods are used to discover which system states are possible; deductive methods are used to discover how a given system state can arise. Choosing the deductive direction is appropriate when one undesired outcome must be explained in terms of its contributing causes.

Fault tree analysis works in failure space rather than success space. Failure, especially complete or catastrophic failure, is usually easier to define unambiguously and easier to model as discrete events than success, which tends to involve continuous performance measures and contested definitions. Practically, a system can fail in fewer significant ways than it can succeed, so modeling failure is more economical: a small number of failure models can cover the significant failure modes, whereas success modeling may require many models for differing definitions of success. The analyst therefore frames the study around an undesired event and enumerates the credible ways it can occur, rather than trying to characterize all the ways the system can work correctly.

Before any fault tree is drawn, the system must be defined: its purpose, its discrete elements, and its boundaries. The external boundary separates the system from its environment and fixes the comprehensiveness of the analysis by determining which inputs and outputs are considered. Boundaries may be physical or temporal, and may shift with operating phase or design changes. Boundary choices should reflect the performance aspect of concern and must remain feasible given available time, information, and resources; if the scope is too large to support, the boundary is drawn in and the expected conclusions are reduced accordingly. Boundaries should ideally be set before analysis and held fixed, but may be revised as information emerges. Whatever is chosen must be stated explicitly in the analysis.

The limit of resolution is the internal boundary that fixes how finely the system is decomposed and therefore how deep the fault tree develops. It defines the 'discrete elements' or basic events below which the analyst assumes no knowledge and models no further interactions. Resolution is governed by feasibility and by the goal of the analysis: detail must not be pushed below the level the available system information can support, and if failure probabilities are to be computed, the limit should stop at events for which data are obtainable. Crucially, tree depth follows the system definition rather than driving it. Developing structure that the system description does not actually justify introduces detail the information cannot support and should be avoided. The chosen limit, and any later changes to it, must be clearly recorded.

Many analysis failures arise at interfaces. Where subsystems are built by different groups, failure modes can emerge from their integration that are invisible when parts are viewed separately. To keep integrated analyses consistent, the same fault definitions and the same event symbols must be used across the pieces, and system boundaries and limits of resolution must be stated clearly so hidden faults and inconsistencies surface. Control systems are particularly prone to interface problems and should not be fragmented; where a control input crosses into a model, a placeholder transfer can be left so the control logic is supplied as one coherent unit. Disciplinary differences in viewpoint also create blind spots, so the analyst must remain unbiased and informed enough to recognize interface problems when they arise.

A fault tree is built around a single undesired event, which becomes the top event and is usually a complete or catastrophic system failure state critical from a safety standpoint. The whole tree is then tailored to this top event: it includes only faults that contribute to that particular failure mode and is not a model of every possible system failure or every possible cause. The faults included are the most credible ones as judged by the analyst, not an exhaustive list. Choosing the top event well is decisive. Too broad a top event makes the analysis unmanageable; too narrow a top event fails to give a sufficiently wide view of the system. Because the analysis can be costly, the value of investigating a given top event should be weighed against the consequences of its occurrence.

topic: Fault tree as qualitative logic model
text: A fault tree is a graphic logic model showing the parallel and sequential combinations of faults that lead to the predefined top event. Its building blocks are events connected by gates: a gate's output is the higher event, its inputs are the contributing lower events, and the gate symbol states the logical relationship that the inputs must satisfy for the output to occur. The faults may represent hardware failures, human errors, or any other pertinent contributing events. A fault tree is fundamentally a qualitative model that depicts logical interrelationships; it can be evaluated quantitatively and often is, but quantification does not change its qualitative nature. Construction proceeds downward from the top event toward progressively more basic events until the limit of resolution is reached.

Fault tree work distinguishes 'failure' from the broader term 'fault.' A failure is a basic abnormal occurrence, such as a component not performing when properly demanded. A fault is a higher-order event: it includes failures but also covers cases where a component operates correctly in itself yet at the wrong time or place because of an upstream condition, producing an undesirable system state without any local failure. Thus all failures are faults, but not all faults are failures. Because timing matters, a fault is properly specified only by stating both what the undesirable state is and when it occurs. These 'what' and 'when' specifications must be part of every event description entered into the tree. By convention, events developed further are termed faults, while basic events not developed further are termed failures.

Component faults are classified into three categories. A primary fault is a fault of a component occurring within the environment and conditions for which the component was qualified and designed; it is an internal failure under normal operating circumstances. A secondary fault is a fault occurring in an environment or under conditions exceeding those for which the component was qualified, that is, failure caused by excessive stresses beyond the design envelope. Both primary and secondary faults are generally component failures. A command fault is different: it involves the component operating correctly in itself but at the wrong time or in the wrong place because of an improper signal or command from some upstream source. This distinction matters because primary and secondary faults are basic events, while command faults point back to causes elsewhere in the system.

It is useful to separate components into passive and active types. A passive component contributes statically, transmitting energy, a load, or a signal from one place to another; its failure results in non-transmission or partial transmission of that signal. An active component contributes dynamically, originating or modifying a signal and typically requiring an input or trigger to produce its output; its failure may yield no output or an incorrect output. The distinction guides how each is assessed and reflects a general reliability difference, with active components typically exhibiting substantially higher failure rates than passive ones. These definitions apply to a component's main function, so specific failure modes may not always align with the component's overall active or passive classification.

Three relative concepts organize how events link in a fault tree. A failure effect is why a failure matters, that is, its consequence on the system. A failure mode is exactly what aspect of failure is of concern. A failure mechanism is how a given mode comes about. Mechanisms produce modes, which in turn produce effects. These roles are relative to the level of analysis: one event can be an effect at a higher level, a mode at the middle, and a mechanism at a lower level, because system, subsystem, and component are themselves relative designations chosen to give the problem hierarchy and boundaries. As the tree descends, the analyst's viewpoint shifts continually from mechanism to mode, with each level's mechanisms becoming the next lower level's modes, until basic component failures at the limit of resolution are reached.

Fault tree development proceeds by the immediate cause concept, sometimes called the 'think small' rule. For any event, the analyst identifies its immediate, necessary, and sufficient causes, not its basic or root causes, taking only one step down at a time. These immediate causes become the next set of events, and the procedure repeats on each of them, advancing one level at a time until the limit of resolution is reached. Working in single steps is essential because it guards against skipping intermediate events: jumping directly to a deeper cause can silently omit a contributing fault that lies between. Methodical one-step development therefore provides assurance that no fault event in the chain is overlooked, and it naturally produces the linked structure of AND and OR logic that the tree expresses.

Primary events are events not developed further; they form the leaves of the tree and are where probabilities must be supplied if the tree is to be quantified. The basic event, drawn as a circle, is a basic initiating fault requiring no further development, signifying that the limit of resolution has been reached. The undeveloped event, drawn as a diamond, is a specific fault left undeveloped either because it is of insufficient consequence or because relevant information is unavailable. The conditioning event, drawn as an ellipse, records specific conditions or restrictions applied to a logic gate and is used primarily with the PRIORITY-AND and INHIBIT gates. The external (house) event, drawn as a house, represents an event normally expected to occur, such as a phase change, and so is not itself a fault.

An intermediate event, drawn as a rectangle, is a fault event that occurs because of one or more antecedent causes acting through logic gates; every event that is developed further by a gate is represented this way. Each intermediate event should carry a precise statement of the fault and the conditions under which it is a fault. Transfer symbols, drawn as triangles, are organizational conveniences that avoid duplicating portions of a tree. A transfer-out marks a branch that must be attached elsewhere, and a corresponding transfer-in, possibly on another sheet, indicates where that branch is developed further. Transfers also provide a clean way to leave a defined place for an externally supplied analysis, such as a control system input, so that the supplied logic attaches as one coherent unit.

The OR gate states that its output event occurs if at least one of its input events occurs, and it may take any number of inputs. Its essential property is that causality never passes through it: the inputs do not cause the output. Instead, each input is simply the same output event restated more specifically as to cause, so the output encompasses all of the inputs. The OR gate is therefore a re-expression of the event above it in terms of more narrowly defined contributing events, corresponding to a Boolean union. A practical diagnostic follows from this: if causality appears to pass through an OR gate, the logic is wrong, which usually signals a missing AND gate and improper analysis. OR gates are normally the inclusive variety unless otherwise stated.

The AND gate states that its output event occurs only if all of its input events occur, and it may take any number of inputs. Unlike the OR gate, it expresses a genuine causal relationship: the input faults collectively constitute the cause of the output fault, corresponding to a Boolean intersection. The AND gate says nothing about the antecedents of its inputs. When dependencies exist among the inputs, they must be incorporated into the event definitions wherever they affect the system logic. In particular, if the occurrence of one input alters the system, for example by switching in a standby unit or changing operating modes or stress levels, a later input must be defined conditionally as 'given the occurrence of' the earlier one, and with multiple dependent inputs each 'given' must incorporate all preceding events.

The INHIBIT gate, drawn as a hexagon, is a special case of the AND gate. Its output is produced by a single input, but only when a qualifying or enabling condition is satisfied; that condition is described in a conditioning event drawn to the side of the gate. The output occurs only if the input occurs under the specified condition. The enabling condition is necessary but is not always by itself sufficient: the input must occur while the condition holds, and the conditioning event may specify the portion of the time the output follows when the input is present. This gate is well suited to situations where an event can only happen in the presence of some particular state or circumstance, and it is also commonly used in representing secondary failures that depend on an enabling environment.

Two further special gates refine the basic two. The EXCLUSIVE-OR gate is a special case of the OR gate whose output occurs only if exactly one input occurs, explicitly excluding the case where both inputs occur together. The PRIORITY-AND gate is a special case of the AND gate whose output occurs only if all inputs occur in a specified order, with the required sequence stated in a conditioning event drawn to the side. In practice the need for a strict sequence is seldom encountered. Likewise, for the independent, low-probability events typical of fault tree work, the numerical difference between the exclusive and inclusive OR is generally negligible, so the distinction usually need not be drawn during construction and can instead be handled, if it matters, during quantification.

topic: Ground Rule I writing fault statements
text: Ground Rule I governs how events are written. Every statement entered in an event box must be written as a fault, stating precisely what the fault is and when it occurs. The 'what' specifies the relevant failed or operating state of the component, and the 'when' specifies the condition of the system with respect to that component that makes the stated state a fault. Such statements are often necessarily verbose, and that is acceptable: the analyst should size the box to the idea rather than trimming the idea to fit the box. Words may be abbreviated, but ideas must not be. Precise, complete fault statements are the foundation of a correct tree, since they fix exactly what each event means before any logic is attached beneath it.

Ground Rule II decides how each event is developed. For every boxed fault, ask whether the fault can consist of a component failure. If yes, classify it as a state-of-component fault; if no, classify it as a state-of-system fault. A state-of-component fault is developed by placing an OR gate beneath it and looking for its primary, secondary, and command contributions. A state-of-system fault is developed by seeking its minimum necessary and sufficient immediate cause or causes, which may call for an AND gate, an OR gate, an INHIBIT gate, or sometimes no gate at all. As a general guide, when the energy or stimulus originates from a point outside the component, the event is typically a state-of-system fault. This classification keeps development systematic and consistent.

The No Miracles rule constrains how component behavior is assumed during construction. If the normal functioning of a component would propagate a fault sequence, the analyst must assume the component functions normally, allowing the sequence to pass; one may not rely on an unexpected, fortuitous failure to block propagation. Conversely, if the normal functioning of a component would block a fault sequence, then that normal functioning must be defeated by faults for the sequence to continue up the tree. Equivalently, wherever an AND situation genuinely exists in the system, the model must represent it. The rule prevents both optimistic and pessimistic distortions: the tree captures the system's real logic instead of invoking convenient miracles to stop or to ease the flow of faults.

Two procedural rules enforce methodical construction. The Complete-the-Gate rule requires that all inputs to a given gate be fully and properly defined before any one of those inputs is analyzed further; the tree is developed level by level, finishing each level before descending. The No-Gate-to-Gate rule requires that gate inputs always be properly defined fault events and that gates never be connected directly to other gates. A gate-to-gate shortcut is a sign of sloppy analysis and often reveals that the analyst does not fully understand the system; while such summarization may be acceptable when condensing a finished tree for quantification, it causes confusion during construction. Both rules reflect the principle that a successful tree depends on a clear and complete understanding of the system being modeled.

Because OR and AND gates correspond exactly to Boolean union and intersection, every fault tree has an equivalent set of Boolean equations, with one equation written for each gate relating its output to its inputs. This correspondence lets the rules of Boolean algebra restructure a tree into equivalent forms. A given problem therefore has no single correct fault tree but many equivalent correct forms, since algebraic identities such as distribution can rearrange the structure without changing its meaning. The analyst can exploit this to simplify a tree for clearer understanding or for easier evaluation, and ultimately to transform it into the minimal cut set form used for qualitative and quantitative analysis. The underlying logical content, and in particular the minimal cut sets, is preserved across all equivalent forms.

topic: Minimal cut sets and path sets
text: A cut set is a combination of basic events whose joint occurrence causes the top event. A minimal cut set is a smallest such combination: every event in it is necessary, so if any one of them does not occur the top event does not occur by that combination. The minimal cut sets define the failure modes of the top event and are unique to it regardless of which equivalent form of the tree is used. Single-event minimal cut sets represent single failures that alone cause the top event, while larger sets represent failures that must occur together. The complementary notion is the minimal path set, a smallest combination of basic-event non-occurrences that guarantees the top event does not occur; path sets define the success modes and can be obtained from the dual of the tree.

Minimal cut sets are obtained by translating the tree into its Boolean equations and then performing systematic substitution and expansion, removing redundancy with the distributive law and the law of absorption. Two equivalent procedures exist. The top-down method starts from the top event equation and substitutes downward, expanding until the top event is expressed purely as combinations of basic events. The bottom-up method starts at the lowest gates, successively substituting equations containing only basic events into the gates above them and reducing as it proceeds upward; it is generally more laborious but yields the minimal cut sets of every intermediate event as well as the top event. Both arrive at the same minimal cut set expression. These substitution principles also underlie the computer algorithms used for larger trees.

Once a tree is reduced, several qualitative results follow without any probability data. The minimal cut sets give all unique combinations of basic failures that cause the top event. Ordering these sets by size yields a qualitative ranking of importance, since smaller cut sets generally dominate: single-event sets are listed first, then pairs, then larger ones, because cut set likelihood typically falls sharply as size grows. Cut sets also let design criteria be checked directly; for example, a rule that no single failure shall fail the system is equivalent to requiring no single-event minimal cut sets. Finally, minimal cut sets can be screened for common cause susceptibility by tagging each basic event with shared attributes such as location, environment, manufacturer, or human involvement, and flagging sets whose events all share a common attribute as candidates for further review.
